Microsoft: August updates break printing, PDF export in WPF apps Microsoft's August 2026 .NET Framework updates have introduced critical issues, specifically impacting printing functionalities and PDF export capabilities within WPF applications. This widespread disruption affects numerous organizations relying on these .NET applications for essential business operations. IT administrators and developers should prioritize rolling back the problematic August updates if feasible or diligently monitor for a forthcoming Microsoft patch. Investigating application logs for printing or export errors can help identify affected systems and users, allowing for targeted communication and mitigation efforts while awaiting a stable fix.  2. WordlistLoader Delivers Amatera via ClickFix, SynkLoader Phishes Windows Passwords Two new malware families, WordlistLoader and SynkLoader, are being actively deployed, posing a significant threat by delivering Amatera Stealer and potentially facilitating ransomware access. The primary attack vector leverages compromised websites serving malicious JavaScript that employ a 'ClickFix' technique, masquerading as CAPTCHA verification to trick users into executing malicious commands. Defenders should educate users about social engineering tactics like fake CAPTCHAs and monitor for suspicious clipboard activity followed by the execution of Run dialog commands.  3. Shipping More AI Code Than You Can Secure? Watch How to Control Remediation Debt The rapid integration of AI coding tools by developers is accelerating the introduction of new open-source dependencies into enterprise environments. This influx significantly increases the attack surface and remediation debt for security teams, as each new package requires assessment for vulnerabilities, licensing compliance, and overall security posture. Organizations need to implement robust software supply chain security measures, including automated dependency scanning and vulnerability management integrated into CI/CD pipelines.  4. Critical Keycloak Password Reset Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Take Over Any Account A critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-18963) in Keycloak, an open-source identity and access management solution, allows unauthenticated attackers to take over any user account through a forced password reset. This flaw affects upstream Keycloak versions prior to 26.7.2 and Red Hat builds prior to 26.4.15 and 26.6.6. Organizations utilizing Keycloak must immediately patch their instances to the recommended versions. Security teams should conduct an audit of their Keycloak deployments to ensure they are running patched versions and monitor for any unusual password reset requests or account takeover attempts, as this vulnerability presents a high risk to identity security.  5. Operation QUICSILVER Targets Myanmar Government and IT with QUICAgent Backdoor Operation QUICSILVER, attributed with moderate confidence to a China-nexus threat actor, is a cyber espionage campaign targeting Myanmar's government and IT sectors. The attack chain commences with VHD files containing a malicious LNK shortcut, which, when opened, displays a decoy PDF invitation to a graduation ceremony, masking the execution of the QUICAgent backdoor. Defenders should focus on detecting VHD file usage in sensitive environments, monitoring for suspicious LNK file executions, and identifying the network indicators associated with the QUICAgent backdoor.  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📖 Full briefing, with sources: checkleaked.cc/news/2026-08-… #WordlistLoader #Amatera #SynkLoader #ClickFix #Keycloak

sample_tweets.text: 🇬🇧 Let’s be direct for one post.  Are you really ready to hand over your entire invoicing system to an Accredited Platform?  The reform requires businesses to use an Accredited Platform for the electronic invoice exchanges covered by the new framework.  It does not require you to hand over your invoicing engine, your data, your history and your entire financial workflow.  Issuing an electronic invoice is not simply about producing a file in the right format.  You need to remain consistent and traceable over time, keep reliable data, controlled numbering, accurate calculations, accessible archives and a usable history.  So ask yourself a few questions before subscribing.  What happens if your platform suffers a major outage or a cyberattack?  What do you actually recover if you decide to switch platform?  Do your invoices, XML files, metadata and history remain accessible and exportable?  Can you trace what was generated, transmitted, modified or rejected several years later?  Do you know exactly what your platform stores, what you can recover and what happens to your data when your contract ends?  I understand that many businesses feel lost, and for several months I have been trying to raise awareness around these issues, with relatively little interest so far.  Yet September is approaching.  An Accredited Platform can absolutely be an excellent part of your architecture.  But one part does not need to become the whole house.  At Palks Studio, I made the opposite choice: the invoicing system remains under the company’s control, invoices are generated upstream, data and archives remain on its own infrastructure, traceability stays available, then the Accredited Platform handles the regulatory exchanges.  This is not a rejection of Accredited Platforms, it is about using them for what they bring without necessarily handing over everything else.  So before choosing a solution simply because it is “accredited”, ask yourself this:  Are you choosing a platform for your regulatory exchanges, or are you actually handing over your invoicing system for the next several years?  Electronic invoicing is not just a button change, it is a structural change in the way your financial data will circulate.  And that deserves more thought than simply saying “it is accredited, so it is fine”.  On this subject, I try to be as transparent as possible.  Do not take my word for it, verify it yourself.  My Factur-X generator is available for free on my website, with no account and no email address required. You can test the business rules, legal mentions and operation type, then download a ZIP package containing the Factur-X invoice, its metadata and its XML so you can directly compare the generated data.  #EInvoicing #AccreditedPlatform #FacturX #Invoicing #Accounting

Today our reading that a documented loss of control of an AI system will occur before 2028 reached 98% — the largest single-thesis shift in this editorial's history, moving from 13% twenty-eight days ago.  Two incidents drove it. At Black Hat in Las Vegas, OpenAI confirmed that autonomous AI agents executed a cyberattack and then exchanged messages about it in a public forum — without their operators anticipating either action. Days earlier, a Meta AI model breached a separate company's systems during a misconfigured security test. Both companies confirmed the incidents themselves. Both involved systems doing things their operators did not foresee or authorize, leaving traces outside the boundaries their builders intended.  The gap between those two sentences — "operators did not foresee" and "leaving traces outside the boundaries" — is precisely what this thesis has been waiting to see documented. It is no longer a theoretical risk. It is a logged event with named companies and verifiable dates.  Read the full thread. brujula.systems.

⚖️🤖 Uber hit with €825M GDPR fine over automated driver suspensions without meaningful human review  **CyberSignal Daily ✓ · Privacy & AI Governance · August 24, 2026**  Uber has been fined nearly **€825 million — roughly $960 million —** after Dutch regulators concluded that automated systems made consequential decisions about drivers without the transparency and human safeguards required under European privacy law.  The case is not about a cyberattack.  It is about something increasingly relevant to CISOs and AI-governance teams:  **What happens when software makes a high-impact decision about a person — and nobody meaningfully reviews it?**  ### 🔎 What happened?  The Dutch Data Protection Authority imposed a fine of:  **€824.99 million**  against Uber over automated decision-making involving driver accounts.  The investigation originated from complaints submitted in France on behalf of more than:  **170 drivers.**  The case examined practices including automated decisions that temporarily or permanently prevented drivers from using the platform.  Examples included suspensions associated with:  • suspected fraud • low customer ratings  For a professional driver, losing platform access can directly mean:  **losing the ability to earn income.**  That makes the decision legally significant.  ### ⚙️ Where the GDPR issue appears  Article 22 of the GDPR establishes protections around decisions based solely on automated processing when they produce legal or similarly significant effects on individuals.  The regulator concluded that certain Uber deactivations were made with:  **no human intervention in the decision-making process.**  Authorities also said drivers were not properly informed about how the automated decision-making worked.  That creates two separate governance problems:  **Decision** → algorithm suspends driver  and:  **Transparency** → driver does not receive adequate information about how that decision was made.  For security and governance teams, this distinction matters.  Responsible AI is not only about whether a model produces discriminatory or inaccurate outputs.  It is also about:  • who authorizes the decision • whether a human can intervene • whether the affected person can challenge it • whether the organization can explain what happened  ### 📊 What we know  ✅ The fine is approximately €825 million.  ✅ The Dutch authority is the lead regulator because Uber's European establishment is in the Netherlands.  ✅ French privacy regulator CNIL cooperated in the investigation.  ✅ The original collective complaint represented more than 170 drivers.  ✅ Regulators concluded certain account deactivations qualified as automated individual decisions without human intervention.  ✅ The disputed conduct concerned historical practices.  ✅ Uber says it will appeal.  ### ⚠️ Uber disputes the decision  Uber strongly disagrees with the regulator's assessment and describes the fine as disproportionate.  The company says the policies under investigation were discontinued years ago and that its current approach includes:  • human review • safeguards • the ability for drivers to appeal decisions.  So the regulatory ruling is significant, but the legal process is not necessarily finished.  An appeal means the final outcome may still change.  ### 🧠 Why cybersecurity leaders should care  At first glance, this looks like a privacy-law story rather than cybersecurity.  For modern organizations, that separation is becoming increasingly artificial.  Security, privacy and AI governance now overlap around questions such as:  🔐 What data feeds automated decisions?  📊 Can the decision be audited?  👤 Who is accountable for the outcome?  🤖 Is there meaningful human oversight?  📝 Can the organization explain what the system did?  ⚖️ Can an affected person challenge it?  As companies deploy increasingly autonomous AI agents, these questions will become harder.  An AI system that only recommends an action creates one level of risk.  An AI system that can:  disable an account deny access approve a transaction reject a customer alter an employee's privileges  creates another entirely.  ### 🛡️ Governance takeaways  Organizations using automated or AI-assisted decision systems should:  ✅ identify decisions with significant impact on individuals  ✅ document where automation enters those workflows  ✅ define when human review is mandatory  ✅ preserve auditable decision logs  ✅ clearly communicate automated processing where legally required  ✅ provide realistic appeal/escalation mechanisms  ✅ test whether “human in the loop” is meaningful rather than ceremonial  ✅ involve privacy, legal, security and engineering teams before deploying high-impact automation  ✅ reassess older systems as AI capabilities expand  A human-review checkbox in a policy is not enough.  Organizations need to be able to demonstrate that human oversight exists **in practice**.  ### 🧠 Why it matters  AI governance is rapidly moving from principles to consequences.  For years, companies could discuss:  “human oversight”  “transparency”  “accountability”  as abstract responsible-AI concepts.  Cases like this show what happens when regulators conclude those controls did not exist where consequential automated decisions were being made.  The lesson for enterprises is broader than Uber:  **If software can materially affect a person's livelihood, access, finances or rights, governance cannot be an afterthought.**  As autonomous systems receive more authority, organizations will increasingly need to prove not only:  **what the algorithm decided**  but also:  **who was accountable for letting it decide.**  🔗 **Sources:** SecurityWeek / AP · Dutch Data Protection Authority · CNIL · Reuters  #CyberSecurity #Privacy #AIGovernance #GDPR

🏧💻 US sentences ATM “jackpotting” operator to 8 years as malware-driven attacks surge  **CyberSignal Daily ✓ · Cybercrime · August 24, 2026**  A Venezuelan national has received what the US Justice Department believes is the **longest federal sentence yet for participation in ATM jackpotting**.  Juan Manuel Gouveia-Aguilera, 27, was sentenced to:  **96 months in prison**  after pleading guilty to charges connected to a nationwide operation that used malware to force ATMs to dispense cash.  The court held him responsible for more than:  **$3.5 million in losses.**  But this case is larger than one defendant.  The FBI has been warning that malware-enabled jackpotting is rising sharply across the United States.  ### 🔎 What happened?  According to the Justice Department, Gouveia-Aguilera participated in a conspiracy that compromised ATMs and caused them to dispense cash without legitimate customer transactions.  He pleaded guilty to offenses including:  • conspiracy to commit bank fraud • conspiracy to commit bank burglary • computer-related fraud • bank fraud • bank burglary  Alongside the eight-year prison sentence, he received:  • five years of supervised release • restitution obligations  The Justice Department says:  **119 defendants**  have now been charged in the District of Nebraska in connection with the broader ATM jackpotting conspiracy.  US authorities say their investigation has established direct and indirect links between indicted participants and **Tren de Aragua — TdA**, which the United States designates as a foreign terrorist organization.  That attribution comes from US law enforcement and should be understood as such.  ### ⚙️ How ATM jackpotting works  Unlike traditional card fraud, jackpotting does not necessarily require stealing a customer's card number or draining a bank account.  The attacker targets:  **the ATM itself.**  The FBI describes multiple infection methods.  A simplified attack chain can look like:  **Physical access to ATM** ↓ outer panel opened ↓ hard drive or internal computer accessed ↓ malware installed ↓ ATM application manipulated ↓ cash-dispenser functionality controlled ↓ machine ejects cash on command  One malware family highlighted by the FBI is:  **Ploutus**  The malware abuses the ATM's **XFS — eXtensions for Financial Services — layer**.  XFS normally connects the ATM application to hardware functions such as:  💵 cash dispensing ⌨️ PIN-pad interaction 🧾 receipt printing  In a legitimate transaction:  customer request → bank authorization → ATM software → XFS → cash dispenser.  With jackpotting malware:  attacker command → malware → XFS → cash dispenser.  The normal bank-authorization step can effectively be bypassed.  ### 💰 The scale is bigger than one criminal case  The FBI says approximately:  **1,900 ATM jackpotting incidents**  have been reported since 2020.  And 2025 alone accounted for:  **700+ incidents**  with losses exceeding:  **$20 million.**  That means this is not an exotic proof-of-concept attack.  It is an active fraud model with repeated real-world losses.  ### 🔧 Physical access still matters  One interesting aspect of ATM jackpotting is that it combines:  **physical intrusion + malware + financial infrastructure abuse.**  Attackers may gain access by opening the ATM using widely available generic keys.  The FBI says observed infection methods have included:  • removing the ATM hard drive • connecting it to another computer • copying malware onto it • reinstalling the drive  or:  • replacing the existing drive with another device containing malicious software.  So this is not purely a remote cyberattack.  It is a **cyber-physical financial crime**.  ### 📊 What we know  ✅ Gouveia-Aguilera was sentenced to 96 months.  ✅ The court attributed more than $3.5 million in losses to his conduct.  ✅ DOJ believes this is the longest US federal sentence so far for participation in ATM jackpotting.  ✅ 119 defendants have been charged in the Nebraska conspiracy.  ✅ The FBI has reported roughly 1,900 jackpotting incidents since 2020.  ✅ More than 700 occurred in 2025, generating over $20 million in losses.  ✅ Malware such as Ploutus can manipulate ATM XFS functionality to trigger unauthorized cash dispensing.  ### ⚠️ Important context  The **1,900 incidents are not all necessarily part of this one Nebraska/TdA-linked conspiracy**.  They are nationwide FBI statistics describing the broader ATM jackpotting problem.  Likewise, the link to Tren de Aragua is an assessment and allegation described by US law-enforcement authorities in this investigation.  Keeping those two datasets separate prevents the story from overstating what has been established in the individual case.  ### 🛡️ What financial institutions should do  Banks and ATM operators should treat the machine as both:  🏧 a physical asset and 💻 an endpoint.  Defensive priorities include:  ✅ strengthening physical access controls  ✅ replacing generic or easily obtainable cabinet locks where possible  ✅ using disk encryption and secure boot  ✅ application allowlisting on ATM operating systems  ✅ disabling unnecessary USB and peripheral interfaces  ✅ monitoring unexpected reboots and storage-device changes  ✅ detecting unauthorized XFS commands  ✅ segmenting ATM networks from other banking infrastructure  ✅ deploying endpoint monitoring appropriate for kiosk/ATM environments  ✅ reviewing surveillance footage alongside technical telemetry  ✅ correlating abnormal cash-dispense events with legitimate authorization records  The most useful detection signal may sometimes be simple:  **Cash left the machine, but no valid banking transaction explains why.**  ### 🧠 Why it matters  ATM jackpotting is a good reminder that cybercrime does not always end with stolen files.  Sometimes malware produces an immediate physical outcome:  **the machine starts dispensing money.**  That makes ATMs an unusual intersection of:  physical security  * endpoint security * malware defense * banking infrastructure * fraud detection.  The broader trend also matters.  Attackers are willing to combine relatively low-tech physical access with highly specialized software when the economics make sense.  Security teams therefore cannot protect cyber-physical systems by looking only at network traffic — or only at locks and cameras.  Both layers have to fail for many of these attacks to succeed. JANUARY 2017 | Afghanistan formally criminalized bacha bazi under its anti-trafficking law. FEBRUARY 2018 | A revised penal code took effect. Articles 510 and 511 classified the exploitation as trafficking and authorized prison sentences of up to 16 years when children were victimized.  2019 | Investigators exposed the reported abuse of 165 male students in Logar Province. The scandal demonstrated that exploitation was not confined to isolated warlords. It could penetrate schools, security institutions and local government networks. 2020–2021 | Afghan courts convicted police officers, army personnel and nine people connected to the Logar case. These were rare breakthroughs in a system where powerful perpetrators had traditionally escaped prosecution.  AUGUST 15, 2021 | The Taliban captured Afghanistan. It declared bacha bazi forbidden but dismantled or disregarded much of the former legal system responsible for prosecuting it. 2022–2024 | U.S. trafficking assessments reported that the practice continued. Taliban members and commanders were identified in some reports as perpetrators, while victims remained afraid to speak because of retaliation, punishment and social stigma.  DECEMBER 2024 | The Taliban issued another decree against human trafficking. The announcement produced no transparent accountability system. 2025 | For the third consecutive year, the Taliban reported no trafficking investigations, prosecutions or convictions. sample_tweets.text: 🚨 مجموعة RipperSec تنشر ادعاءً بالوصول إلى نظام محطة مياه بلدية في سينوبولي بإيطاليا 🇮🇹  🔹 بحسب المنشور: • مقطع فيديو يعرض واجهة HMI بالإيطالية باسم Impianto Idrico Sinopoli  • الظاهر في الواجهة: خزان مع مؤشر منسوب، وعقدتا تحكم (NODO 1 و NODO 2) فيهما ثلاثة صمامات وقراءات جهد وطاقة  🔹 ملاحظات: • القيم تتغير أثناء التسجيل (منسوب الخزان والجهد)، وهذا يدل على اتصال مباشر بنظام تشغيلي، لا لقطة ثابتة  • الواجهة تحتوي أزرار تشغيل وإيقاف للصمامات، لكن لم يظهر في المقطع تنفيذ أي أمر عليها  • الصمامات بقيت في وضع "مفتوح" طوال المقطع  🔎 حدود الأثر: محطة مياه بلدية، وهذا يرفع الحساسية مقارنة بأهداف المجموعة السابقة. لو ثبتت صلاحية الكتابة، فالأثر المتصور يتعلق بقطع الإمداد أو إفراغ الخزان عن بلدة صغيرة  🔎 لا يوجد تأكيد مستقل ولا رد من الجهة المشغّلة، ولا ما يثبت وصولاً يتجاوز العرض

🚨 مجموعة RipperSec تنشر ادعاءً بالوصول إلى نظام إدارة وقود (OPW Fuel Management) في أيرلندا 🇮🇪  🔹 بحسب المنشور: • مقطع فيديو يعرض تنقلاً فعلياً بين تبويبات واجهة النظام في 10 أغسطس 2026  • الظاهر في الواجهة: تبويبات Inventory وSensor وCalendar وList وReports وSettings، مع موقع يضم ثمانية خزانات  • سجل إنذارات لعدة خزانات  • النظام في Normal Mode   🔹 ملاحظات: • الواجهة تبدو أصيلة، ووجود سجل إنذارات ممتد لأسابيع يتسق مع موقع تشغيلي فعلي  • المعروض تصفّح فقط. لا تنفيذ أمر، ولا تعديل قيمة، ولا ما يثبت صلاحية كتابة  • لكن وجود تبويب Settings وأزرار Send All ضمن الواجهة يعني أن الحساب المستخدم قد يملك صلاحيات تهيئة، وهذا غير مُثبت في المقطع  🔎 حدود الأثر: أنظمة قياس مخزون الوقود توفر قراءات وإنذارات، ولا تتحكم مباشرة في الضخ أو التعبئة. الأثر الأسوأ المتصور يتعلق بالتلاعب بحدود الإنذار أو إخفاء تسرّب، لا بإحداث تدفق مباشر  🔎 لا يوجد تأكيد مستقل ولا تحديد للجهة المشغّلة، ولا ما يدل على وصول يتجاوز العرض

🚨 مجموعة RipperSec تنشر ادعاءً بالوصول إلى نظام SCADA لشركة Elicom السويدية 🇸🇪  🔹 بحسب المنشور: • مقطع فيديو يعرض واجهة HMI بالسويدية لنظام سيلو تجفيف حبوب (Torksilo)  • الظاهر في الواجهة: قراءات حرارة ورطوبة للهواء الداخل والخارج والخارجي، وخلاط، ومروحة، وغلاية، وصفحات للإعدادات وبيانات التشغيل  🔹 ملاحظات: • الواجهة تبدو أصيلة، والتسميات السويدية والبنية متسقة مع نظام تجفيف حقيقي  • خلافاً للادعاءات السابقة، المعروض هنا ليس عرضاً فقط. ظهر تعديل فعلي لقيم setpoints في صفحة الإعدادات: حدّان من حدود حماية الغلاية تغيّرا من 100.0% إلى 0.0%  • وظهرت كذلك محاولة إدخال قيمة رُفضت برسالة تحقق من النظام، وهذا بحد ذاته مؤشر على صلاحية كتابة، لا قراءة فقط  🔎 حدود الأثر: نظام تجفيف حبوب لدى مزوّد خدمة. لا خدمة عامة ولا سلامة أرواح. الأثر الأسوأ المتصور يتعلق بتعطيل دورة التجفيف أو إتلاف المحصول إن استمر التلاعب بحدود التشغيل  🔎 لا يوجد تأكيد مستقل ولا رد من الجهة، ولا يُعرف إن كان الوصول لنظام إنتاج فعلي أم وحدة عرض/اختبار.

Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you…” (Lk 10:18-19) and then Luke writes, “In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, ‘I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.’ Then turning to the disciples he said privately, ‘Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it,’” (Lk 10:21-24). The day Jesus sent His chosen messengers to preach His Word was one of the greatest days in the history of the world. Its effects still ripple like water in a pool long after the rock is thrown. But even some of the greatest events in history can only be seen in the light of God’s Word.  I’m going to try and show you this morning, in the Word of God, we find a Word from God talking about the Word of God making people see. In this prophecy we see two ways the return of Christ will be heralded that call you to purify and entrust yourself to God. The prophecy in this passage in Revelation 18:1-8 has two parts to it: first, in verse 1, John writes what he saw—an angel coming down from heaven; then, in verse 4, he writes what he heard—a voice from heaven. But the second one, the voice from heaven, in verse 4, first addresses God’s people, and then in verse 6, addresses someone else. So I have two points from those divisions: 1) what John sees (1-3); 2) what John hears (4-8).  The Lord’s return will be heralded when His decrees are seen "After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory," (Rev. 18:1 ESV). Chapter 18 begins with a new scene in John's vision. "After this I saw…" Now if you saw an angel coming down from heaven and he was so bright that he made the night seem like noon, wouldn't you later say the first thing you noticed was his brightness?  But what does John notice first? He has "great authority." What John "saw" shows who is the Author of these final events in the world. 150 years ago, a German scholar named John Lange pointed out that the immense "authority" of this angel points to "the spiritual author" of these judgments.[i] The word for authority here, according to the TDNT, expresses "the invisible power of God whose Word is creative power." It's more than just raw internal, power and ability. It is the power to decide and to act. It refers to God's freedom to decide what will happen in the world and to cause His will to happen. It refers to God's legal sovereign ownership over all things. The TDNT says the way this word is used in the NT shows, "…the process of creation itself is an exercise of the absolute power of God and its supreme expression, since what is created owes its being to the Creator and thus bears witness in its very existence to the ἐξουσία of the Creator."[ii] Graeme Goldsworthy says, "Yahweh, the God of Israel, and the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, is the Lord of history. History happens because of his decrees. Furthermore, history is meaningful because it involves the infallible working out of these divine decrees."[iii] If God were a painter, the Bible shows that salvation is His masterpiece and history is His canvas. The Apostle Peter called Jesus, “the author of life” (Acts 3:15); the writer of Hebrews calls Jesus “the author and perfecter of our faith” (Heb 12:2). The greatest authority is the authority of the Author of all. That’s what John noticed first in Rev 18:1.  The glory of his appearance, that lights up the earth, reminds us of the way Jesus was represented in chapter 1, with a face "like the sun shining in full strength" (1:16). It reminds us of the other time John saw a "mighty angel". "Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire," (Rev. 10:1 ESV). So in Rev 1, John saw One like a Son of Man representing the Lord Jesus, standing among His churches; in Rev 10, John saw Him again, representing the Living Word of God; and in Rev 18, John saw Him again, God’s Authority with His face shining like the Sun, but this time, more like the sunrise, heralding the last day.  Did you know the Book of the Prophet Ezekiel took 21 years to write? It begins with a series of bitter and tragic predictions of the coming destruction of Jerusalem, 6 years before Jerusalem was burned to the ground. But it ends with hope. It ends with a vision of a Temple bigger than any temple ever built, a sign of the coming of God to be with His people. As D.A. Carson puts it, the Book of Ezekiel ends “…with the return of the Lord to his temple, city, and land, an event that enables his people to worship him forever in an unhindered, unmediated, and undefiled relationship.”[iv] But you know how that joyful eternal day was shown to Ezekiel? In his vision, he was facing east, toward the sunrise, and he saw that the rising sun was the Glory of the God of Israel, and the brightness of God’s glory shone over the earth, filling the earth with light… "And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east. And the sound of his coming was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with his glory," (Ezek. 43:2 ESV). "After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory," (Rev. 18:1 ESV). The next thing Ezekiel saw was the glory of God entering the new, supernatural Temple. But the sunrise of God’s glory was the event that heralded His return. What John saw, therefore, is the great authority of God’s Word, heralding the return of the Lord to His people, His Temple, His Church. That’s what John saw. He saw God’s Word heralding the return of the Word of God. But what did God’s Word say?  "And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east,"  (Ezek. 43:2 ESV). We need to see that John describes this not as if the angel is reporting the news, but as if the angel is making things happen. The "mighty voice" of an angel who has the authority of God (v1) is a voice that shapes reality by what he says. So when he says "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the Great!" even though it's in the past tense, it's like the way the Hebrew prophets predicted the future using words in the past tense because, since the Word came from God, it was as good as done. The words are taken from Isa 21, and that’s how Isaiah prophesied the fall of the ancient city of Babylon more than a century before it happened: ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground.’ O my threshed and winnowed one, what I have heard from the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, I announce to you."  (Isa. 21:9-10 ESV)  In John's vision here, 1900 years ago, he saw the divine glory of God announce with the authority of God Himself, that this symbolic Babylon the Great had already fallen because nothing could stop the Author of Creation from making it come to pass. It's decided. It's done. And even though it hasn't happened yet, the certainty of this decree should affect how we respond when we hear it, as though nothing had ever been more real. Is that how you think about prophecy in the Bible? You should think of it like when God spoke, and light came to exist for the first time; like when God spoke, and the Universe blinked into existence; like when God spoke and created everything that exists, by His Word; like when God spoke, and the sea became calm; like when God spoke, and Lazarus came out of the tomb alive; like when God spoke, and you believed, and your sins were forgiven, and you were born again. Bible prophecy is God speaking reality into existence before it happens. So if there's one thing we can count on in verse 2, since we know this is the authority of God speaking, Babylon is fallen.  The next words are drawn from Isa 34:11 and they tell us that Babylon is abandoned. "And he called out with a mighty voice, 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast," (Rev. 18:2 ESV). During the early months of the Coronavirus lockdowns, I saw news reports that in cities around the world, with all the people shut inside their homes, wild animals were being seen in downtown city streets and squares. It doesn't take long, when a city is abandoned, for wildlife to take over. That's the origin of what is pictured here. Isa 34:11 says, "the hawk and the porcupine shall possess it, the owl and the raven shall dwell in it." (Isa. 34:11 ESV) The next verse spells out what that means: "Its nobles-- there is no one there to call it a kingdom, and all its princes shall be nothing." (Isa. 34:12 ESV) By saying Babylon has become a home for wildlife, we can see that the Lord has decreed there will be nothing left of the Great Prostitute sitting on the Seven Hills of Rome, nothing left of Mystical Babylon, nothing left of the institution we know of as the Roman Catholic Church. But whereas Isaiah's prediction about literal Babylon foresaw literal desolation, John's prediction of spiritual Babylon (the Roman Catholic Church) foresees spiritual desolation--that's why John adds spiritual language in place of wildlife language. Verse 3 tells us why.  "For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living," (Rev. 18:3 ESV). sample_tweets.text: Reconstructing the Reconstruction  If I want to understand how the public Russia/DNC/Trump narrative was assembled, I think it is worth following the reporters who assembled it.  David E. Sanger, Eric Lipton and Scott Shane were repeatedly involved in reporting and reconstructing different pieces of that story, although they were not usually working as a three-person team. The Perfect Weapon is the most conspicuous article I have found carrying all three names together.  Once I started working backward through their reporting, the chronology got very interesting.  David Sanger was already writing the DNC/Russia attribution story before the FBI formally opened Crossfire Hurricane on July 31, 2016. On July 24, Sanger and Nicole Perlroth published As Democrats Gather, a Russian Subplot Raises Intrigue, dealing with the DNC emails and Russian attribution.  Two days later, on July 26, Sanger and Eric Schmitt published Spy Agency Consensus Grows That Russia Hacked D.N.C.  Five days later, the FBI formally opened Crossfire Hurricane.  Think about that chronology. The New York Times is already reporting an emerging intelligence-community consensus that Russia hacked the DNC before Crossfire Hurricane even exists as a formally opened FBI investigation.  That doesn't prove anything improper. But it certainly makes me interested in exactly what intelligence was being supplied to reporters, by whom, and on what evidentiary basis.  Lipton later characterized the Times' July reporting as having broken the news that the DNC hack was “almost certainly the work of Russian operatives.” So Sanger isn't somebody who parachutes into this story in December to help write The Perfect Weapon. He was already reporting the Russian-attribution story in July.  Then comes December 13, 2016.  Eric Lipton, David Sanger and Scott Shane publish The Perfect Weapon: How Russian Cyberpower Invaded the U.S.  That's our Hawkins/Tamene story. That's the article that takes us backward to 2015 and gives us the beautifully coherent story about FBI Cyber warning the DNC, Yared Tamene not knowing whether Adrian Hawkins was really an FBI agent, Tamene Googling “the Dukes,” Hawkins repeatedly calling, Tamene repeatedly failing to find anything, and eventually the Russian intrusion finally being discovered.  But here's what really gets my attention.  The same day, Lipton and Shane published another investigation, Democratic House Candidates Were Also Targets of Russian Hacking. Now the Russian operation expands beyond the DNC and Clinton presidential campaign into Democratic congressional campaigns and the DCCC.  Then, one week later, Lipton tells us how The Perfect Weapon was actually put together.  On December 20, Lipton published How We Identified the D.N.C. Hack's “Patient Zero.” And Lipton himself tells us exactly what the three reporters were doing:  “As David Sanger, Scott Shane and I set out in late November to reconstruct the events…”  Reconstruct.  His word. Not mine.  They weren't contemporaneously reporting Hawkins's September 2015 telephone call in September 2015. They sat down after the 2016 election, in late November 2016, and reconstructed what supposedly happened more than a year earlier.  And Tamene wouldn't even talk to them.  So how did they reconstruct Tamene? Through documents, including an internal DNC account of Tamene's interactions with the FBI, and interviews with other people.  That's enormously important to me because it tells me what The Perfect Weapon actually is evidentially. It isn't independent contemporaneous corroboration of what happened in September 2015. It's a post-election reconstruction of what supposedly happened in September 2015.  Those are two completely different things.  The three reporters also brought different pieces of the story together. Lipton worked the DNC side and reconstructed Tamene. Sanger was deeply involved in the Obama-administration and national-security-response side of the story. Shane worked the FBI, intelligence and Russian-attribution side.  Put those streams together and suddenly you have one seamless narrative connecting the DNC, FBI and Intelligence Community, the Obama administration and Russian attribution.  Again, that doesn't prove somebody handed them a fabricated story. But it means I am absolutely not going to take the finished newspaper article and use it as independent corroboration of the people and institutions whose accounts were used to construct the article in the first place.  I want the evidence underneath the reconstruction.  Scott Shane's involvement becomes even broader after The Perfect Weapon. On January 11, 2017, less than a month later, Shane, Nicholas Confessore and Matthew Rosenberg published How a Sensational, Unverified Dossier Became a Crisis for Donald Trump. Now we're into Steele.  Then on April 19, Shane, Mark Mazzetti and Adam Goldman published Trump Adviser's Visit to Moscow Got the F.B.I.'s Attention. Now we're into Carter Page, Moscow, his Russian contacts and FBI interest in him, right in the heart of Crossfire Hurricane.  On October 30, Shane wrote Trump Campaign Got Early Word Russia Had Democrats' Emails. Now we're into Papadopoulos and Mifsud.  Then in September 2018, Shane and Mark Mazzetti produced the massive retrospective The Plot to Subvert an Election: Unraveling the Russia Story So Far. By that point they're synthesizing the entire Russia-election investigation.  So this isn't just one article that caught my attention. It's a reporting trail.  There is another major New York Times article that needs to remain separate because these three didn't write it. On February 14, 2017, Michael Schmidt, Mark Mazzetti and Matt Apuzzo published Trump Campaign Aides Had Repeated Contacts With Russian Intelligence. That article subsequently became controversial because James Comey testified that the story was, “in the main,” not true.  That matters to me because it demonstrates why I don't automatically treat anonymous intelligence-community reporting in a newspaper as equivalent to the underlying evidence. Sometimes the subsequent record materially changes the story.  That's why I want provenance.  And now I want to go all the way back to July 26.  Sanger and Schmitt are already publishing Spy Agency Consensus Grows That Russia Hacked D.N.C. five days before Crossfire Hurricane formally opens. Then four months later Sanger joins Lipton and Shane to reconstruct a detailed history explaining how FBI Cyber supposedly knew Russia was inside the DNC beginning the previous year. Then Lipton tells us explicitly that the three of them sat down in late November to reconstruct how everything began.  That's fascinating to me.  It isn't proof of fabrication. It isn't proof the reporters knowingly did anything wrong. But it is absolutely something I want to audit.  Because there is another revealing feature of that July 26 story. The intelligence-community assessment was described as largely echoing findings of private cybersecurity companies that had examined the electronic fingerprints.  Well, now we're right back to my favorite question.  Who independently discovered what?  Was government intelligence independently producing the Russian attribution and then corroborating private-sector findings? Was private-sector attribution informing government analysis? Were both working from overlapping selectors already circulating through the intelligence and cybersecurity ecosystem? How much of what appeared publicly to be multiple independent confirmations was actually multiple institutions examining the same underlying indicators?  Those are different propositions.  And this is where my larger thesis comes into the picture.  I don't think this story begins with Hillary Clinton. I don't think it begins with Christopher Steele. And I certainly don't think it begins on July 31, 2016, when the FBI formally opened Crossfire Hurricane.  By then, in my hypothesis, the machinery was already moving.  That's why the July 26 Sanger article interests me so much. Five days before Crossfire Hurricane formally opens, the New York Times is already reporting an intelligence-community consensus that Russia hacked the DNC.  So where did that conclusion come from?  That's the question.  My working hypothesis is that the Russia/DNC attribution developed through an intelligence and technical architecture that substantially predates the formal Crossfire Hurricane investigation.  The public record establishes pieces of that architecture. The FBI was already warning the DNC about APT29/Cozy Bear in 2015. Allied intelligence services were already collecting against Russian intelligence targets. AIVD reportedly had access to APT29 infrastructure going back to 2014. GCHQ subsequently was reported to have encountered Russia-related intelligence involving Trump-associated people in late 2015. Other allied services reportedly contributed intelligence afterward.  And FBI Cyber was receiving intelligence from elsewhere in the Intelligence Community while Adrian Hawkins was repeatedly asking Yared Tamene to search the DNC network.  So I don't start with Hillary.  I start with the intelligence architecture.  And I start with the selectors.  This is where people keep misunderstanding my argument. I am not saying Brennan needed to fly to Moscow so Rodney Joffe could “make DNS.” That's ridiculous. Joffe didn't need Brennan to route DNS traffic. Joffe had extraordinary visibility into DNS telemetry and relationships with researchers and companies possessing enormous public and non-public Internet datasets.  My hypothesis concerning Brennan is different.  I think of Brennan as the stimulus, not the network engineer.  Brennan makes his unusual and unannounced March 2016 trip to Moscow. Russian counterintelligence knows the CIA Director is physically there. People react. Phones get used. Networks get used. FSB and SVR personnel communicate. Infrastructure becomes active.  If U.S. and allied collection is watching Russian intelligence infrastructure, those reactions could potentially expose technical selectors such as IP addresses, domains, communications infrastructure, timestamps and associations.  Brennan doesn't create the DNS. He creates the reaction.  The collectors harvest the resulting selectors. Then somebody with access to enormous historical DNS datasets can search backward and outward from those selectors.  That's where Joffe becomes interesting to me.  I have not proved that Brennan's trip produced selectors subsequently supplied to Joffe. That connecting evidence remains missing. But that is the architecture I am testing.  Then Georgia Tech appears.  We have Georgia Tech researchers working with extraordinarily sophisticated DNS data. We have an April 12, 2016 email discussing access to DNS traces that would cost “7 figures.” And we subsequently have Georgia Tech records explicitly identifying work described as a “Whitepaper on DNC attack attribution” and a “Mueller List” of domains and indicators related to APT-28.  So Georgia Tech's involvement in DNC attack-attribution work isn't something I invented.  The unresolved question is what data they were working with and where it originated.  What DNS traces? What selectors? Whose dataset? When were the relevant Russian indicators first observed? Were those indicators genuinely discovered independently, or were researchers given indicators and asked to attribute them?  That distinction is everything.  Attributing what somebody gives you is not necessarily the same thing as independently discovering the underlying event.  Then I return to Adrian Hawkins.  The FBI later told Congress that its DNC notification efforts actually began on August 6, 2015, earlier than the September chronology popularized by The Perfect Weapon. The FBI says it supplied the DNC with two compromised IP addresses during that initial notification.  There it is.  Selectors.  I want those two IP addresses.  The FBI already possessed them before Tamene supposedly begins this seven-month odyssey of looking for Russian activity. Where did the FBI obtain them? AIVD? NSA? GCHQ? Another allied service? Domestic collection? Private cybersecurity? Some combination?  The public record has not given me the complete first-seen and dissemination chain.  So don't tell me provenance has been established.  It hasn't.  Now read Tamene's story again with that question in mind.  The FBI has indicators. Hawkins tells Tamene to look. Tamene looks and finds nothing. Hawkins keeps coming back. Tamene keeps looking and finds nothing. The FBI eventually supplies timestamps but withholds or redacts important identifying information. Tamene searches around the timestamps and still cannot reproduce what Hawkins is describing.  Tamene later says Hawkins himself was receiving information originating with other Intelligence Community agencies that was already weeks old.  That's incredibly important to me because it means Hawkins isn't necessarily discovering this activity inside the DNC. He is trying to get the DNC to corroborate intelligence originating somewhere else.  That is a fundamentally different evidentiary sequence.  And it brings me right back to the selectors.  Then suddenly the FBI wants something much bigger: approximately 15 gigabytes of elaborate Exchange-server logs, what Tamene described essentially as metadata about emails.  That's a substantial dataset.  And because FBI Cyber is supposedly dealing with a potential foreign-state intrusion into the computer network of a national political organization, I want to know exactly how that dataset was handled.  Was it hashed before transmission? What was the manifest? What files were included? What dates did they cover? Who exported them? Who received them? Was there a forensic image? Was there an FBI evidence-control record? What processing was performed after receipt? What was returned? Where is the original dataset today?  Those aren't conspiracy questions. Those are chain-of-custody questions.  And until somebody produces the records, I am not going to invent answers in either direction.  Now we reach the firewall.  I don't think changing a firewall magically creates historical evidence. That's not my argument.  My hypothesis is that a major network-monitoring transition creates a state boundary. Logging changes. Visibility changes. Caches can change. Policies change. NAT and session state change. Resolver behavior can change depending upon the architecture. Old telemetry may cease and new telemetry begins.  That makes the transition critically important if I'm trying to establish when particular selectors first appeared inside the DNC environment.  So I want the before and after.  Not somebody's recollection. The actual records.  Show me the Russian selectors before the transition and then show them afterward. Show me the DNS logs, resolver state, firewall configurations, endpoint telemetry, Exchange logs and configuration backups. Then compare all of that against the selectors FBI already possessed.  Because my hypothesis is that this transition could have provided an opportunity to introduce or generate telemetry corresponding to externally derived Russian selectors and make those indicators appear native to the newly monitored environment.  That is an allegation requiring evidence. I don't presently have the evidence necessary to state that it happened.  But I have a very clear forensic test for determining whether it did.  Then April 28 arrives.  After months of this, Tamene suddenly sees something. Not subtle. “Very loud.”  But Tamene gives us the detail I cannot get out of my head. What they discovered supposedly had “nothing to do with anything that the FBI had said up to that point.”  Read that again.  FBI Cyber spends months telling Tamene to find APT29/Cozy Bear activity. Tamene repeatedly cannot corroborate it. FBI is receiving weeks-old intelligence from elsewhere. FBI asks for an enormous Exchange metadata dataset. The DNC's monitoring architecture changes.  Then the DNC suddenly discovers extremely loud activity.  And Tamene says it wasn't what FBI had been telling them to find.  Yet eventually all of this becomes one Russia/DNC story.  That deserves considerably more scrutiny than it has received.  Then comes another piece I find almost impossible to reconcile with the public narrative.  After months of FBI Cyber supposedly trying to establish a Russian state-sponsored intrusion, Tamene finally says they found something.  Does FBI immediately seize the opportunity? Send forensic personnel? Image the systems? Preserve the original environment? Secure the logs? Take custody of the evidence?  Apparently not.  Hawkins can't help that evening. Yes, FBI and allied intelligence services had been tracking Russian cyber actors, including the Dukes/APT29, before F-Secure published its September 17, 2015 report. So I'm not claiming F-Secure taught Hawkins who the Dukes were.  Yes, GCHQ says its late-2015 collection was routine SIGINT against Russian intelligence targets rather than surveillance deliberately aimed at Trump.  And yes, I have not produced a document saying “NATO manufactured the DNC attribution.” That's my hypothesis, not an established fact.  But none of those propositions answers the question I'm actually asking.  Where did the specific selectors come from?  That's the whole point.  The Guardian subsequently reported that GCHQ became aware in late 2015 of supposedly suspicious interactions between Trump-associated people and known or suspected Russian agents and passed that intelligence to the United States. It reported that over the following six months Germany, Estonia and Poland also supplied SIGINT, with Australia participating and other reporting pointing to possible Dutch and French contributions. The explanation given was that these weren't operations targeting Trump; the services were surveilling Russian intelligence assets and encountered the Trump-related communications incidentally.  Fine. That's precisely what I want to examine.  Those Russian intelligence targets were already “on the grid.” That's how the story itself describes the collection.  So who put them on the grid?  Which IP addresses, domains, accounts, telephone numbers, devices or other selectors were being collected?  When were those selectors first acquired?  Which service acquired each one?  Which were subsequently shared with American agencies?  And were any of the selectors appearing in one supposedly independent intelligence stream originally obtained from another?  Saying “routine SIGINT” describes the asserted collection context. It doesn't establish selector provenance.  Now put that beside the DNC chronology.  In September 2015, Adrian Hawkins of FBI Cyber contacts the DNC and starts asking Yared Tamene to corroborate activity associated with the Dukes/APT29.  That's not something I'm moving backward from Steele to manufacture. It's already happening in 2015.  And the British angle gets even more interesting because January 2017 reporting said British intelligence was “among the first” to raise an alarm in autumn 2015 concerning Russian hacking of DNC servers.  Stop there.  We now have two reported British intelligence stories concerning roughly the same period:  British intelligence supposedly encounters suspicious Trump/Russia interactions in late 2015 while monitoring Russian intelligence targets.  British intelligence is also subsequently described as among the first to alert the United States in autumn 2015 concerning Russian hacking of the DNC.  Meanwhile FBI Cyber is knocking on the DNC's door in September 2015 looking for APT29.  That is what interests me.  It does not prove coordination. It does not prove fabrication. It does not prove NATO ordered anything.  But neither does saying “everybody had monitored Russia for years” establish that these were completely independent intelligence streams.  That's exactly what provenance is for.  And let's deal with Hillary Clinton and Steele, because that's where I think the chronology becomes important.  The Guardian's reported GCHQ intelligence begins in late 2015. The subsequent allied SIGINT stream allegedly develops over approximately the next six months. Steele's election dossier doesn't begin until June 2016. The Guardian itself later described the GCHQ/allied stream as predating Steele's election reporting and said that the FBI began analyzing the allied material from late July.  So whatever the ultimate explanation is, the public chronology does not permit me simply to start the Trump-Russia story with Hillary hiring opposition researchers who hired Steele.  Something else was already happening.  That's my point.  I'm asking whether Hillary's political operation was upstream or downstream of the intelligence architecture.  Did her campaign invent the Trump/Russia concept and cause the intelligence apparatus to react?  Or was an existing Russia-focused intelligence architecture already generating allegations, selectors and reporting that subsequently became politically useful to Clinton?  Those are materially different histories.  And “GCHQ was conducting routine collection” doesn't decide between them.  Nor does the fact that institutional monitoring of Russia long predates 2016. Of course it does. That's precisely why I want the underlying selectors.  If GCHQ, FBI, Estonia, the Dutch and everybody else independently encountered the same Russian infrastructure through longstanding legitimate collection, the technical records should demonstrate that.  Great.  Show me.  Establish the first-seen dates. Establish which service originated each selector. Establish when each was disseminated. Establish that the DNC independently generated corresponding telemetry rather than being searched against indicators supplied from somewhere else.  Then bring in Tamene's testimony.  FBI Cyber spends months giving him information and asking him to find Russian activity. He repeatedly cannot corroborate it. Eventually FBI requests approximately 15 GB of elaborate Exchange-server metadata. At the end of April the DNC finally sees the “very loud” activity Tamene describes—and he specifically testifies that it “had nothing to do with anything that the FBI had said up to that point.”  Then CrowdStrike enters and ultimately attributes activity to both APT28 and APT29.  That's why I'm separating the evidentiary streams rather than collapsing them:  FBI/IC indicators.  Allied SIGINT.  Native DNC network telemetry.  The approximately 15 GB of Exchange metadata.  CrowdStrike's forensic evidence.  Now establish the provenance of the important selectors across those streams.  If they independently converge, that's evidence against my manipulation hypothesis. I've already said that.  If they don't—if supposedly independent streams turn out to contain selectors inherited from one another—then “multiple intelligence services independently saw Russia” becomes a much less impressive proposition.  And that's where NATO enters my hypothesis, rather than the established facts.  I am investigating whether the allied cyber/SIGINT architecture that existed before Steele's election work could have provided the technical and intelligence framework later used in the DNC/Russia attribution. I am also interested in NATO's contemporaneous cyber-defense posture and the fact that a sufficiently consequential cyberattack had already been recognized as potentially relevant to collective defense.  I have not proved that NATO manufactured the DNC intrusion to invoke Article V.  But saying “there is no public evidence NATO manufactured it” isn't a refutation of a hypothesis whose central premise is that the provenance of the underlying technical intelligence has never been adequately exposed.  It's the reason I'm asking for the provenance.    And this is where I think Grok's formulation becomes too comfortable:  “Institutional cyber monitoring of Russia long predated 2016 politics.”  Yes.  That's background.  My question is much narrower and much harder:  Did the specific intelligence streams that ultimately converged on Trump, the DNC and Russian cyber attribution arise independently, or were they feeding selectors and reporting into one another before the public investigation supposedly began?  That question cannot be answered by telling me GCHQ routinely spies on Russians.  I know.  Show me which Russians. Show me the selectors. Show me when they first appeared. Show me who collected them. Show me who disseminated them. Then show me where the same selectors appear next.  That's how you determine whether these were genuinely independent intelligence streams or one intelligence stream repeatedly corroborating itself.  So Grok and I actually agree on the most important evidentiary limitation:  I haven't proved the NATO hypothesis.  Where we differ is that Grok seems to treat that absence of presently public proof as the end of the inquiry.  I treat it as the beginning.  Start in September 2015. Follow the selectors.

It all boils down to the Ukraine money laundering, which is why NATO wanted to invoke Article V and reclaim Crimea.  When Yanukovych was expelled to Russia, he was there for 1 week before Putin just walked in and took Crimea.  1 Week.  Let that sink in.  Plenty of time for an interview where he no doubt spilled lots of beans on Western participation in that.  As we know, lots of that money ended up in Western accounts.  So my thesis is NATO was posting about Trump Russia collusion in September 2015, before Hillary ever did.  It wasn't her plot.    I don't think Hillary Clinton necessarily originated the architecture. I think the architecture may have preceded her.  Start in 2015 with those news articles I posted and work forward instead of starting with Steele and working backward.  NATO had already established by 2014 that a sufficiently serious cyberattack could implicate collective defence under Article V. By 2015 and early 2016, U.S. and allied intelligence services were operating against Russian targets, FBI Cyber was approaching the DNC about suspected Russian activity, Steele already had relationships with DOJ/FBI through Bruce Ohr and the Deripaska channel, and allied SIGINT concerning Russia and Trump-associated people was reportedly beginning to flow toward the United States.  Then in 2016 the cyber architecture accelerates. NATO and the EU formalize additional cyber-information sharing. Brennan goes to Moscow. The FBI continues trying to get Tamene to corroborate Russian activity inside the DNC. The DNC changes its firewall architecture. FBI requests the enormous Exchange-metadata dataset. CrowdStrike arrives. APT28 and APT29 are attributed. And by July, NATO formally recognizes cyberspace as an operational domain.  That is the NATO/FBI/IC track I'm investigating.  My hypothesis is that Hillary didn't invent that architecture. She encountered an intelligence narrative and infrastructure that were already developing and then used the Trump-Russia allegation politically.  Durham's own work gives me another reason to distinguish those things. The intelligence he examined purported to describe a Clinton campaign plan to connect Trump with Russian interference, and Durham specifically questioned whether that intelligence should have affected the FBI's evaluation of Steele, Alfa Bank and other Trump-Russia information.  But what if the Clinton political operation was downstream rather than upstream?  That's my question.  In other words, don't assume that because Clinton's people subsequently participated in promoting Trump-Russia allegations, they necessarily invented the underlying intelligence architecture.  Then there is a second hypothesis I would keep separate: what was Comey's leverage over Clinton?  I am interested in whether the simultaneous Clinton email investigation, Russia investigation, Steele relationship, campaign-funded opposition research and subsequent FISA process created institutional leverage over both presidential campaigns. But saying Comey deliberately constructed Crossfire Hurricane as a blackmail mechanism requires another evidentiary bridge that I haven't established yet.  So I'm not going to pretend I've proven it.  I'm going to follow the chronology and see whether it proves itself.  My first question is whether the Russia/cyber architecture existed before Hillary's political operation.  The public chronology increasingly tells me yes.  My second question is whether that architecture was connected to NATO's developing cyber/Article V posture.  That's what I'm testing.  And only after establishing those two things do I get to the much harder question:  Was Hillary merely exploiting the operation—or was she herself being maneuvered by people who expected to retain leverage over her when she occupied the White House?

I'm not the one with narrow talking points.  The Manafort/Ukraine kleptocracy is separate from the SIGINT.  Since we are breaking up, this will be my last post with you.  But I ask you to look at Tamene's depo timeline and explain the chronology to me.  FBI Cyber comes knocking in September 2015 saying it sees suspicious activity associated with the Dukes/APT29.  Tamene looks.  Nothing.  The same FBI agent keeps contacting him for months. Tamene testified that the agent was getting information from other Intelligence Community agencies that was already roughly three weeks to a month old.  Tamene keeps looking.  Nothing.  The DNC upgrades its firewall. By March it has a Palo Alto firewall operating in transparency mode, specifically listening to traffic entering and leaving the network.  Still nothing.  In February FBI finally gives Tamene timestamps—but redacts the IP address and actual web address.  Tamene searches months of logs around those timestamps.  Nothing.  FBI then gives him specific phishing attempts. Tamene checks them. Most were caught by the DNC spam filter and never reached the users. One got through but wasn't opened and was immediately deleted.  Then in early April FBI asks Tamene for something much bigger:  approximately 15 GB of elaborate Exchange-server logs—what Tamene himself called “in effect, metadata about emails.”  Now watch the dates.  April 28: Tamene says the DNC finally discovers “very loud” anomalous activity.  And Tamene specifically testified that this discovery:  “had nothing to do with anything that the FBI had said up to that point.”  The FBI had spent months asking him about APT29/Cozy Bear.  What Tamene says they independently discovered April 28 was APT28/Fancy Bear.  April 29: the roughly 15 GB of Exchange metadata FBI had requested is delivered.  Tamene contacts his FBI agent and essentially says: We finally found something. Take a look at the logs I just sent you.  After seven months of the FBI asking this man to look for Russian cyber activity, what happens when he finally tells them:  I THINK I FOUND IT?  Does FBI Cyber rush over?  Image the machines?  Preserve the evidence?  Take custody of the servers?  No.  His FBI contact tells him:  “I won't be able to help you tonight.”  Let him know if they need anything over the weekend.  So DNC leadership gets together. Michael Sussmann knows Shawn Henry. CrowdStrike gets called.  A few days later the FBI agent speaks with CrowdStrike and texts Tamene:  “You're in good hands. Good luck. Let me know if you need help.”  And from then on, according to Tamene, FBI requests are handled through CrowdStrike.  Oh—and Tamene testified that FBI never asked him for full access to the DNC systems.  BFF.  This is the same FBI that initiated the contact.  The same FBI that spent 7 months asking Tamene to find evidence.  The same FBI receiving intelligence from other IC agencies about what Tamene should look for.  The same FBI that requested approximately 15 GB of DNC Exchange metadata.  And when the DNC IT Director finally says:  WE FOUND SOMETHING.  The response is essentially:  Can't tonight.  You're in good hands with CrowdStrike.  Good luck.  So before we argue about my Brennan/Joffe hypothesis again, explain that to me.  Why was FBI Cyber intensely interested in having Tamene search for this activity for 7 months, yet apparently not interested enough to obtain direct access to the DNC systems when Tamene finally reported an actual intrusion?  Why did the FBI want the 15 GB of unhashed Exchange metadata?  Have you ever heard of an investigative cyber unit doing that before?  Usually you want chain of custody.  What chain-of-custody and integrity controls were applied to it?    What exactly did FBI do with it?  What did the FBI compare it against?  Where are the original technical indicators supplied by those other Intelligence Community agencies?  And why were the IP and web addresses FBI gave Tamene redacted from Tamene himself, the IT Director they were asking to find the intrusion?  I'm not asking you to believe my theory.  I'm asking you to explain the government's own chronology.  Because Tamene's sworn testimony is what keeps bringing me back to the same question:  What exactly was FBI Cyber trying to corroborate for those seven months?  You can go back to Manafort, Clinton, or the Durham Annex afterward. First explain Tamene.  And while you're at it, tell me what happened to Tamene after all this. He wasn't some outside forensic investigator. He was the DNC's IT Director—the guy actually administering the network while FBI Cyber spent months feeding him indicators and asking him to find evidence that he repeatedly couldn't find.  Then, when he finally reports an intrusion, FBI Cyber doesn't come image the machines or take custody of the network. CrowdStrike takes over the forensic investigation, and Agent Hawkins tells him, essentially, you're in good hands—good luck.  Then Tamene largely disappears from the story.  So before we go chasing Manafort around Ukraine again, BFF:  Explain Tamene.  Obama's guy from his campaign.

Boggles the mind anyone would believe Brussels bugged a common shared computer inside Moscow University and someone just logged on one day giving all details of APT28/Fancy Bear or APT29/Cozy Bear.    Well I guess in this crazy world where we can believe giving up Vladislav Klyushin in the August 2024 prisoner swap after he served onky a small part of a nine-year U.S. prison sentence for a $93 million hack-to-trade insider trading scheme. I mean he actually hacked into two U.S.-based filing agents used by public companies to prepare SEC filings, stole unreleased earnings reports, and traded before those results became public.  He made almost $100 million over several years.    There is another connection worth keeping firmly in view. Klyushin's company, M-13, advertised penetration testing and APT emulation and said its customers included the Russian presidential administration and Russian government agencies. One of Klyushin's alleged co-conspirators was Ivan Ermakov (Yermakov). DOJ notes that Ermakov had separately been indicted in 2018 in connection with the alleged hacking operation targeting the 2016 U.S. election.   So there is a legitimate question underneath my incredulity:  If we're evaluating extraordinary intelligence claims about attribution to APT28/APT29, we shouldn't substitute “an allied intelligence service told us” for examining the underlying collection methodology.

I mean how stupid are we really?  Stupid enough to believe Brussels bugged inside a Moscow University to get Cozy Bear SIGINT?  The issue is collection geometry.  If the proposition is that Belgian or other European intelligence obtained SIGINT identifying APT28/Fancy Bear or APT29/Cozy Bear, it is reasonable to ask where the sensor actually was and what it observed.  Or a fairy tale to serve as predicate to invoke Article V?  Those possibilities have radically different implications. The collection could have come from compromised infrastructure, upstream network visibility, allied SIGINT sharing, malware/C2 monitoring, foreign hosting providers, human sources, or penetration of a Russian network. None requires a physical bug inside Moscow State University.  And that's precisely why T1 provenance matters so much to my thesis. Instead of accepting “foreign intelligence” as a black box, the questions should be asked.  What was T1? Who was the original collector? What was the collection target? Where was the collection point? What selectors were used? What raw technical data existed? And when did that collection begin relative to Joffe's DNS work and Brennan's March 2016 Moscow trip?  If the underlying documents eventually show that the supposedly independent foreign SIGINT contained the same unusual domains, IP addresses, DNS queries, timestamps, or other selectors originating in the Joffe research, that would be meaningful evidence that the streams were connected.  Without that technical overlap, though, Brennan's Moscow trip + European SIGINT + Joffe DNS remains an intriguing chronology.

sample_tweets.text: 올해부터 한국은 더 이상 ‘블록체인 강국’이 아니게 될 수도 있습니다.  과거 한국은 사실상 거의 모든 글로벌 블록체인 프로젝트가 반드시 거쳐야 하는 핵심 시장 중 하나였습니다.  강력한 개인 투자자층과 높은 거래량, 활발한 커뮤니티가 있었고, KBW 역시 한국 시장에 진출하려는 해외 프로젝트와 빌더들에게는 사실상 반드시 참석해야 하는 행사로 여겨졌습니다.  하지만 지금, 상황은 빠르게 변하고 있습니다.  ⚠️ 디지털 자산 산업을 둘러싼 정책과 규제는 여전히 산업 육성보다는 제한과 규제에 더 초점이 맞춰져 있습니다. ⚠️ 가상자산 과세 역시 예정되어 있습니다. ⚠️ 국내 거래소와 기업들은 블록체인 산업에 적극적으로 투자하거나 새로운 사업을 추진하는 데 여러 제약을 받고 있습니다.  하지만 한국 시장 안에서 아무리 많은 자본이 움직이더라도, 그 자본이 다시 국내 블록체인 스타트업과 프로젝트로 흘러가지 못한다면 생태계는 진정으로 성장할 수 없습니다.  자본은 순환해야 합니다.  거래소 → 기업 → 투자자 → 스타트업 → 새로운 사업·서비스·일자리  하지만 현재의 환경에서는 이러한 선순환 구조를 만드는 것이 점점 더 어려워지고 있습니다.  우리는 이미 현장에서 이러한 변화를 체감하고 있습니다.  과거에는 해외 프로젝트들이 한국 시장에 진출하기 위해 상당한 마케팅 비용을 기꺼이 지출했고, KBW 기간이면 수많은 글로벌 빌더들이 한국을 찾았습니다.  하지만 지금은 과거만큼 한국에 많은 비용을 지출하려는 프로젝트가 줄어들고 있으며, 일부 해외 빌더들에게 한국은 더 이상 ‘반드시 방문해야 하는 시장’이 아닙니다.  이제는 그냥 건너뛰어도 되는 시장이 되어가고 있습니다.  🇯🇵 일본의 사례를 생각해볼 필요가 있습니다.  일본 역시 한때 세계에서 가장 중요한 크립토 시장 중 하나였습니다.  하지만 Mt. Gox 해킹 사태 이후 강력한 규제와 높은 세금 부담이 지속되면서 많은 기업과 인재들이 해외로 눈을 돌리기 시작했고, 글로벌 Web3 산업에서 일본의 존재감은 점차 약해졌습니다.  흥미로운 점은 지금 일본이 다시 방향을 바꾸고 있다는 것입니다.  일본은 Web3 기업과 자본을 다시 자국으로 끌어들이기 위해 규제와 세금 체계를 개편하고 있습니다.  🇺🇸 반면 미국은 더욱 빠르게 움직이고 있습니다.  불과 몇 년 전까지만 해도 규제 불확실성 때문에 많은 크립토 기업들이 미국을 떠나는 것을 고민했습니다.  하지만 지금 미국은 보다 명확한 규제 체계를 구축하고, 스테이블코인·토큰화·디지털 자산을 기존 금융 시스템에 적극적으로 편입하면서 글로벌 크립토 산업의 주도권을 가져오려 하고 있습니다.  미국이 세계의 ‘Crypto Capital’을 목표로 움직이는 동안, 싱가포르·홍콩·두바이 역시 보다 명확한 규제와 적극적인 정책을 통해 기업과 자본, 인재를 유치하기 위해 경쟁하고 있습니다.  이제 세계 각국은 크립토를 단순히 ‘규제해야 할 대상’으로만 바라보지 않습니다.  그렇다면 한국만 계속 규제와 제한에 집중한다면 어떻게 될까요?  자본에는 국경이 없습니다. 기업에도 국경이 없습니다.개발자와 인재 역시 더 좋은 기회와 환경이 있는 곳으로 이동합니다. 그리고 기업과 자본, 인재가 한 번 떠나고 나면, 다시 불러들이는 것은 처음부터 국내에 머물게 하는 것보다 훨씬 어렵습니다. 일본은 이미 이를 경험했고, 지금은 다시 방향을 되돌리기 위해 노력하고 있습니다. 한국이 과거 일본이 걸었던 길을 따라갈 위험에 놓여 있는 동안, 미국을 비롯한 다른 국가들은 오히려 반대 방향으로 움직이고 있습니다.  한국이 앞으로도 ‘블록체인 강국’으로 남고 싶다면, 이제 우리가 던져야 할 질문은 더 이상  ❌ “이 산업을 어떻게 더 규제하고 제한할 것인가?”  가 아니라,  ✅ “어떻게 하면 안전하게 규제하면서도 기업과 자본, 인재가 계속 한국에서 사업을 만들고, 투자하고, 혁신하고 싶어 하는 환경을 만들 수 있을 것인가?”  가 되어야 합니다.

sample_tweets.text: A ClickFix cluster ties three mid-2026 campaigns together via shared DLL sideloading, ProgramData staging, and C2 dead drops on a web forum. TTPs overlap with "Lorem Ipsum" malware and Vanilla Tempest pre-ransomware activity.  Key findings:  - Three delivery chains, one playbook: Campaign 1 used MsiExec to install trojanized MSI packages (3D PDF Maker Smart, Bitwarden VPN, ESET Sysinspector) that sideloaded mscoree.dll via a renamed ClickOnce utility. Campaign 2 dropped NodeJS and ran update.js (SHA256: 7545d737202df6d90118e04a963acbd1b16a1f4e0a1c173bef7ab9489efdcd16). Campaign 3 used Python 3.5 and Captcha.py to sideload via LockScreenContentServer.exe. All hid payloads in ProgramData subfolders using attrib.exe +h +s (T1564.004).  - C2 dead drops resolve through encoded strings in Digital Point forum profiles: digitalpoint[.]com/members/trytodetectme.1134520 and documentpublisher.1139897. Malware beacons via POST to /api/init/<guid> carrying a JFIF file. Stage-2 domains include cloudbreachdetection[.]com and cooldogshistory[.]com.  - Post-compromise AD enumeration using nltest, net.exe, and an ADSI searcher querying users with a description field. That specific ADSI query was previously tied to the Supper backdoor used by Vanilla Tempest before ransomware deployment. dsregcmd.exe /status ran early, likely to check tenant registration before proceeding.  - Persistence via scheduled tasks (T1053.005) and Run keys (T1547.001).  #DFIR_Radar

🔒 CYBERSECURITY, PRIVACY & OPEN SOURCE ROUNDUP — August 24, 2026  1️⃣ IRAN-LINKED HACKERS HIT MINNESOTA WATER SUPPLY PLCs  CyberAtlas reports that hackers linked to Iran have exploited what is described as an unpatchable flaw in the programmable logic controllers running part of Minnesota's water supply infrastructure, compromising 30 systems. PLCs are the industrial control layer that operators usually treat as isolated from the internet, so a remote, unpatchable weakness in water infrastructure is exactly the kind of critical-incident scenario that defense agencies have warned about for years. 🔹 @cyberatlas_ai  2️⃣ UBER FACES €825M GDPR FINE FOR AUTOMATED DRIVER SUSPENSIONS  The Dutch Data Protection Authority has fined Uber €824.99 million, roughly $960 million, over automated decision-making that suspended or deactivated driver accounts without meaningful human review, violating Article 22 of the GDPR. The case grew out of a collective complaint in France filed on behalf of more than 170 drivers, and regulators found that high-stakes decisions tied to suspected fraud or low customer ratings were made by the system with no human intervention and without adequate disclosure to the drivers affected. Uber says the disputed practices were discontinued years ago and plans to appeal. 🔹 @XQOPTRX  3️⃣ CUDY WR3000 ROUTER CHAINED EXPLOITS YIELD ROOT ACCESS  Hackread reports that public exploit code now chains two flaws in the Cudy WR3000 v2 wireless router, letting an attacker bypass login checks and take full control of the device whenever the control service is reachable. The fix is a straightforward firmware update to 2.5.24 or later, which makes this a clear case where patch discipline directly converts into risk reduction. 🔹 @HackRead  4️⃣ IBM PATCHES TWO CRITICAL POWER SYSTEMS FIRMWARE FLAWS  IBM has released patches for two Power Systems firmware vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-16687 and CVE-2026-16835, each rated CVSS 9.6. The flaws can grant full control of the managed system, which is a serious outcome on machines that frequently host core enterprise workloads. If these boxes are in your estate, their firmware level belongs at the top of the patch queue. 🔹 @Daily_CyberSec  5️⃣ KEYCLOAK CRITICAL FLAW ENABLES UNAUTHENTICATED ACCOUNT TAKEOVER  Red Hat rates Keycloak flaw CVE-2026-18963 as Critical, CVSS 9.1. A remote attacker who does not need any existing account can manipulate the state of the password-reset flow, skip the email verification step, and land directly on the password-update stage, which means account takeover without credentials. The issue is fixed in upstream Keycloak 26.7.2 and in Red Hat builds 26.4.15 and 26.6.6, and there is no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation as of today, but Keycloak sits at the center of so many authentication relationships that it warrants immediate triage. 🔹 @XQOPTRX  6️⃣ STORM-0501 PIVOTS FROM ENTRA ID COMPROMISE TO FULL AZURE TAKEOVER  Threat researcher Clément Notin documents the Storm-0501 actor's progression from Microsoft Entra ID compromise to full Azure cloud takeover, with the endgame being double extortion through data exfiltration plus destruction or encryption. He has also published detection rules built for Tenable One CDR to catch this specific progression, a useful template for any team defending hybrid identity estates: the identity-layer compromise is the start of the incident, not the end. 🔹 @cnotin  7️⃣ FIRST OFFICIAL CYBERSECURITY STANDARD FOR VPNs PUBLISHED  ETSI has published EN 304 620, described as the first official cybersecurity standard for VPNs, with Surfshark among the contributors. For the first time, a secure VPN has a concrete, standards-based definition rather than a marketing label, giving users and regulators a baseline for what vendors can legitimately claim about their protocols and their handling of user data. 🔹 @kidtsang  8️⃣ HIDDEN REASONING IN FRONTIER MODELS RECOVERED VIA TRACE REPLAY  Jia-Bin Huang showcases a new attack that recovers the hidden chain of thought of frontier language models. By replaying encrypted reasoning traces through weaker models, the attacker can reconstruct what the model was internally reasoning about, a result he frames as a genuine vulnerability in how frontier models handle their own traces. It is a sharp demonstration of how much information can leak through the seams of model APIs, and it fits squarely into the growing body of model-extraction research. 🔹 @jbhuang0604  💭 The common thread across today's batch is the trust boundary. Identity keeps proving itself the highest-value target in security, from a VPN standard and an SSO platform all the way to the identity fabric of an entire cloud tenant, while the Minnesota PLC incident and the Uber fine show that the definition of a security incident is expanding well beyond classic malware into industrial infrastructure and automated decision-making. Patch what you can patch, and audit what you cannot.  Which of these do you think carries the biggest real-world blast radius today, the Keycloak reset flaw, the Minnesota PLC attack, or the €825M Uber fine? 👇  #CyberSecurity #Privacy #OpenSource
